newsitem.title: USA: White House DC plan has problems - Hill tax panel.
newsitem.headline: White House DC plan has problems - Hill tax panel.

text.p: The White House's proposed tax incentives to stimulate economic development in District of Columbia are fraught with problems, Kenneth Kies, chief of staff of Congress' joint tax committee, said Thursday.

Kies offered the view at a hearing by the House Government Reform Committee's subpanel on D.C. on the $300 million Economic Development Corporation that is a key part of a multi-billion-dollar D.C. revitalization package proposed by the White House on Jan 14.
Clinton said the new corporation would get $50 million to set up shop and $250 in tax breaks and other incentives it could use to encourage companies to local in the city.
For instance, District businesses could get a 40 percent tax break on the first $10,000 they pay each low or moderate income resident in the first year of employment, according to the plan.

Kies said that in order for employers to claim employment credits, they must meet three tests. The people they hire must live in D.C. the entire first year of employment, live in a poor area and expect to make less than $28,500 each annually, and do all the work they were hired for in the city.
"Every one of these tests requires extensive recordkeeping and verification procedures," Kies said. "There is a high probability of noncompliance -- intentional, as well as unintentional."

Also, if the employee moves out of the District at any time during the year, no credit would be available to the employer, Kies said. Business owners would have to "speculate" when they hire the person whether they could claim the special tax incentives at the end of the year, he said.
The bottom line, Kies said, is that high compliance costs and uncertainty built into the proposals limit their effectiveness.

Kies also said the tax incentives probably will not spur a major increase in economic growth in the D.C. metropolitan area as a whole. However, targeted impoverished areas of the city could see "significant revitalization," he said.

Also, under the plan, the city could make substantial use of its private activity bond volume cap within four or five years, Kies said. "These bonds will provide a cheaper source of funds for both 'start-ups' and business expansion within the District," he said.

Rep. James Moran, a Democrat who represents some of D.C.'s closest Virginia suburbs, said the White House plan does not do enough to restructure the "punitive" D.C. tax code. He noted that the corporate income tax rate in D.C. is 9.975 percent, compared to six percent in Virginia and seven percent in Maryland.

"A typical information technology company would pay $22,078 in income tax in the District, Moran said. "In Virginia, that same firm would pay $13,280. The D.C. corporate property tax rate is $2.15 - more than twice that of surrounding jurisdictions," Moran said.
"If D.C. is to attract new business, it must stop chasing business away," he said.

Rep. Tom Davis, R-Va., chairman of the subcommittee, said of the White House plan, "I question whether some of the provisions will achieve the stated goal." He said Congress wants to give the District tools to encourage business not only in distressed communities, but downtown as well.
